pr_body:
Implementation of writeable JSON DOM including support for C# `dynamic`.

Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/47649

Notes:
- The ability to have extension properties by of type `JsonObject` is not implemented in the PR to help reduce review size. That support will come after this PR is in and will allow an extension property of the form:
`[JsonExtensionData] public JsonObject ExtensionData {get; set;} `
- `MetaDynamic.cs` contains internal code to support C# `dynamic`. As a follow-up to this PR, additional tests may be added to increase coverage here and\or that code refactored to reduce some lower-level expression-based code.
- Test coverage is nearly 100% except for `MetaDynamic.cs` as mentioned above.
- The internal use of `JsonObject`'s `System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<,>` will be replaced with a dictionary that supports ordering semantics so inserts\removes are deterministic with list-based semantics; ordering is nondeterministic with `Dictionary<,>`.

comments:
May I suggest to change ``Task WriteToAsync(Stream,`` to ValueTask, just as in ParseAsync?
Maybe also switch the order of cancelationtoken and Options in ``ParseAsync``, having the token at the end is more common.
Yes. Token should always be at the end.

@Tornhoof

> May I suggest to change Task WriteToAsync(Stream, to ValueTask, just as in ParseAsync?
> Maybe also switch the order of cancelationtoken and Options in ParseAsync, having the token at the end is more common.

The current design section "Features not proposed in 6.0" states that we don't want to have every permutation that `JsonSerializer.Deserialize` already has. This is for varying reasons but one is to that the overloads add clutter at least for non-common cases -- e.g. the design has static "Parse()" method on all 4 node types in order to prevent casts, so every time we add another "Parse()" overload it has to go into 4 classes...

A work-around is to use the `JsonSerializer.SerializeAsync()` directly.

Also note that currently the design does not purport to implement true async read\write behavior with nodes. If this is an important concern, please reply with scenarios. Internally the serializer for non-node scenarios (POCOs and collections) does have true async behavior on both deserialize and serialize meaning async calls to a `Stream` via `ReadAsync()` \ `WriteAsync()` are called often to keep the internal buffer size smallish. However, nodes do not support this -- this means during deserialize the `Stream` is drained upfront (mostly because `JsonElement` is used which has that behavior) and since `JsonElement` doesn't have any existing async-based "write" methods, the existing serializer-based `SerializeAsync()` must be used that will write to a growable buffer until finished, then write the whole thing to the `Stream` in one call.

Re: `JsonArray`, we may want to reconsider interfaces like `IEnumerable<T>`, `IList<T>`, and others. With the current design, even if we hide the explicit interface implementations for unwanted methods like _Contains_, LINQ will reintroduce them into the calling context.

> Re: JsonArray, we may want to reconsider interfaces like IEnumerable<T>, IList<T>, and others. With the current design, even if we hide the explicit interface implementations for unwanted methods like Contains, LINQ will reintroduce them into the calling context.

If we just implement `IEnumerable` for interop with LINQ (and not `IEnumerable<T>`, doesn't that hurt "dot syntax" for querying or navigating up\down since a cast to `JsonNode` would need to be used?

The utility of the other members of `IList<T>` that are currently explicitly implemented is probably low, and overkill, but may still be useful in some scenarios including immediate recognition of the contract as well as potential usage of existing extension methods like a Reverse() or Sort().

review_comments: Should we set `_lastKey` and `_lastValue` here?
It seems `dynamic` semantics are only supported when using `JsonObject`. What happens when other node types are treated as dynamic i.e setting/getting properties is attempted?
The dynamic feature allows you to call members on `JsonArray` and `JsonValue` (e.g. `jArray.Add()`). If an invalid member is specifies, `RuntimeBinderException` is thrown.
Is it possible and/or worth it to clear the list in this same loop (e.g. would assigning `null` to `List[i]` be sufficient here?)
A call to base.Clear() is necessary to remove all of the items efficiently (e.g. Count will return zero).

Can we suppress this in our suppressions file, e.g. [this](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/c377f4152351dfbe16099317f553b87d2ce24b6b/src/libraries/System.Data.Common/src/ILLink/ILLink.Suppressions.xml#L70-L75)? A bit cleaner, I think.

---

Is it a high priority for usages of the node types to be ILLinker-friendly?
I'm open to this, but don't think it's necessary with this PR.
Considering for a future PR is fine with me.
Could we use `ICollection<JsonNode>.Count` on `JsonArray` to get the count?
I'll add a line to compare against `obj.MyArray.Count` as well.
Turning `_dictionary` into a cocrete type means that we could probably use the `Dictionary<K,V>.AddRange` method here, which performs a few optimizations depending on the input.
Sure. When this PR is in, I'll switch over to a custom type anyway (for deterministic ordering semantics) that internally will use a dictionary with direct access.

Is there a reason why this is not using a `Dictionary<string, JsonNode?>` directly?
`JsonArray` is using a `List<JsonNode?>`  https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/51025/files#diff-e7e94002d7a28a31460df75e87474da2bbea3d91bb90bc873da332bb704dd3cfR19

Note that after this PR is in, the direct use of `Dictionary<,>` will be replaced with a dictionary that has deterministic ordering semantics (so insert\delete produce JSON in an expected manner) but which will still implement `IDictionary<,>`.

At that time, a direct reference will likely be made instead of using the interface.
Could it be valid in the future to want to replace/unbind from the parent?
Unbinding happens when an element is removed via Remove() or replaced via an indexer.
Could this be `private`? Same for `TrySetMemberCallback`.
Is it invalid for the user to pass an options instance that will not be honored?

It is valid; the consumer likely doesn't care whether or not the nodes were created from parsing JSON (which doesn't use the options), or are new (which uses the options to produce the JSON). This is similar to how we handle extension data - the parsed JSON is held by JsonElements which are written out the same way and options\custom converters\etc are not called.
Out of curiosity, why do we need to remove this?
Oh I see, it's being replaced by dynamic altogether.
Or > Count?

It is correct as written -- `ArgumentException` thrown when  > Count (not `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`), although the wording for that is a bit kludgy: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.list-1.copyto?view=net-5.0
FWIW adding XML docs to explicit interface implementations is not necessary. I believe msdocs will use documentation from the implemented interface. @carlossanlop to confirm.

`ConvertJsonElement` and `TryConvertJsonElement` seem very similar. Could we instead call `TryConvertJsonElement` here, and throw the `IOE` if it returns false? Perhaps we could then delete `ConvertJsonElement`.

Perhaps. The reason is since we delegate to `JsonElement` to obtain the values in `ConvertJsonElement` we leverage the existing validation and exception logic in `JsonElement`. `JsonElement` in some cases throws `FormatException` and in other cases `InvalidOperation` which we would need to duplicate if we combine.
Curious why this is? Based on the rest of the method body I would have expected the output to be valid JSON.

Per review, this was requested by the Azure SDK team. These values are supposed to be human-readable and do not need to be round-trippable JSON. Plus it includes whitespace that normally users don't want for performance.

The `ToJsonString()` should be used to obtain round-trippable JSON.
Got it, thanks.
Is the serialization order guaranteed here (pending an ordered-dictionary-based implementation)?

Yes pending the ordered dictionary which will be added after this PR. Currently the test workswith `Dictionary<,>`, although that technically is not deterministic and only works for add-only cases (not items removed).
Does Newtonsoft.Json have similar behavior in this scenario?

Yes - it also doesn't use the serializer features. Json.NET has a "JsonLoadSettings" class has three properties which control comment handling, duplicate property handling and "line info" handling which essentially is debug information for obtaining the line number and position.
Do you imagine people will run into issues with the somewhat subtle semantics here?

With collection initializers this can occur although I don't see an easy alternative to "force" the options to be specified upfront before "Add()".

Originally, I had a design where the `JsonSerializerOptions` were used instead of `JsonNodeOptions` since those options have a concept of case insensitivity. However, that dependency was removed because tying those options to DOM creation was somewhat confusing since basically only the case insensitivity flag was used and nothing else. However, using `JsonSerializerOptions` like originally proposed could work in this scenario when we implement the ability to change the global options (as is scheduled for v6 I believe).

So if we add the ability to change the global `JsonSerializerOptions` perhaps we also add the ability to change\specify a global `JsonNodeOptions` and that could be used to address this scenario.

I see - yeah we should document this explicitly. 

> when we implement the ability to change the global options (as is scheduled for v6 I believe).

I'm getting more and more scared of doing this due to side effects with the defaults being changed in a way that affects all assemblies in a compilation.

Could we delegate to `Dictionary.ContainsKey` to do the `null` check? We sort of do this today we `JsonSerializerOptions.GetConverter(Type)`, where passing `null` will cause the dictionary lookup to throw. Maybe we should be fixing that instead 🤷
Delegating to dictionary means that the exception will surface 'key' as the offending parameter name.

> Delegating to dictionary means that the exception will surface 'key' as the offending parameter name.

Correct that is the reason why the validation logic is duplicated here.
I believe I saw a similar formatter defined in either `WriteStack` or `ReadStack`. Would it make sense to consolidate into a shared helper method?
The code is different since they operate on different inputs (JsonNode vs WriteStack\ReadStack). Perhaps a strategy or visitor pattern can be applied however although that may be overkill.
Or > Count?
Same as JsonArray\List - ArgumentException thrown in that case (verified via test).
nit: I assume it's also invalid to have a `JsonObject` have a JsonArray property which contains the object itself as an element. Can we codify that in a test?
would it make sense to repeat the assertions in lines 125-126 after the call to `Clear()` has been made?
Nice. Are there other characters that are interesting enough to test?
Do you mean for the property name or for the value? The `JsonNodeOperatorTests.cs` has every value type possible (int, uint, string, char, etc)
Do we need the intermediate `ToList()` here?

Yes since ForEach exists on `List<>`, not `IEnumerable<T>`.

We could add additional constructors to JsonArray to take an `IEnumerable<T>` or `IEnumerable<string>` etc to make this easier and not require ForEach.
Yup we can wait for user feedback here.
Is it possible to have this work in the future?

Yes if we decide we want to ease up on the `GetValue()` semantics and invoke the serializer. That would also require the `JsonSerializerOptions` to be passed in for things like quoted numbers.

We could also add a new method, like Json.NET's `JNode.ToObject()`, to deserialize.
